content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper investigates the use of a wavelet transform to provide
the input to convnet in the context of BCI using EEG data.
While the success of the approach is plausible (using time-frequency
transforms as input to nets in audio is quite common), the paper
has a number of issues.

My first concern is that the paper is not well written (many typos,
latex formatting style, sentences too long and hard to parse). This
harms readability of the contribution.

Now regarding the contribution: given the amount of work on this topic
and the marginal difficulty of the contribution, the only way I see
to convince reviewers is to provide a massive empirical evaluation
that proves a clear win on the state-of-the-art. Unfortunately the
paper reports results on only one dataset with no clear improvement.

I would encourage the author(s) to get some help with writing and
conduct a more thorough evaluation. See for example
the community effort on MOAB (Mother of all benchmarks) for BCI
(https://github.com/NeuroTechX/moabb) that aims to provide a
clear and public baseline.

Remarks on text:

- "which is an affordable solution, noninvasive, easy setup, and portability" -> "which is an affordable solution, noninvasive, with easy setup, and portability"

- "state of the art" -> "state-of-the-art" when used adjective

- check difference between \citet and \citep

then I stopped as there are too many.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper applies CNN architectures and wavelet decomposition of some moderate-dimensional EEG signals from a recent EEG-BCI competition with the aim of using representational compactness to increase classification efficiency while retaining computational efficiency. The motivation is good and the position in the (vast) EEG-BCI literature is appropriate.
However, I see neither a convincing case for computational efficiency (it is still a net requiring large training as opposed to simpler frequency binning / generalized svd methods), nor a convincing case for a classification accuracy breakthrough (results are similar to many other known methods). Furthermore the pictures showing 'activation' patterns are not necessarily revealing nor are they convincingly artifact - filtering. Overall the decision is to reject based on insufficient significance and impact of result - although the paper is otherwise fairly well written and organized.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
EEG-based brain-computer interfaces is a difficult task, as the signal is noisy, vary from subject to subject and classical machine learning techniques are still deficient for certain subjects.
The authors propose a DWT-based deep net, where convolutional layers are applied on a wavelet decomposition of the signal.
To avoid the curse of dimensionality, only half of the wavelet coefficient are used to train the convnet.
A higher dropout is applied to avoid overfit.
The proposed net is evaluated on a dataset and different wavelet transforms are assessed. 

This contribution is not convincing enough. The idea to use DWT is interesting but not new and the results are only tested on one small dataset.
The proposed approach should be applied on different types of BCI task (P300, error potentials, etc), as it is the case in Lawhern et al. (2018) or at least on several datasets of motor imagery, see [1] for example of available datasets.
The results should be compared to state-of-the-art techniques, that is tangent space classification using Riemannian geometry, see [2]. Comparing the results with FBCSP is not enough.

To improve this contribution, the authors could make the following modifications.
The experimental protocol section is not really relevant, as it is already described in the literature and the authors use the data in a common way. The last paragraph of this section is interesting, the rest could be dropped.
The Proposed method section could include a figure to show the sequence of preprocessing applied to signal and the shape of the deep net.
The results part is a bit hard to read as it just a description of the table. A figure with star indicating significant statistical difference could help to ease the reading.

[1] Jayaram, V., & Barachant, A. (2018). MOABB: trustworthy algorithm benchmarking for BCIs. Journal of neural engineering, 15(6), 066011.
[2] Lotte, F., Bougrain, L., Cichocki, A., Clerc, M., Congedo, M., Rakotomamonjy, A., & Yger, F. (2018). A review of classification algorithms for EEG-based brain–computer interfaces: a 10 year update. Journal of neural engineering, 15(3), 031005.
